# Tobit Chapter 12 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
Chapter 12 is the theological climax of Tobit — the angelophany in which Raphael reveals his identity and delivers the book's central moral teaching. 12 divergences were logged across the 22 verses, concentrated in the angelophany section (vv. 11–22) and the wisdom speech (vv. 6–10).

---

## Disagreement Table

| Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | Resolution |
|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|------------|
| 12:1 | Payment instruction phrasing | "See, my-child, to give the-wage...and to add to him [something] beyond [the wage]" | "See to it, my child, that you give...his wages, and add something beyond them" | "make sure you pay the man...what he's owed. Give him more than you promised" | **LOGOS** — clearest and most natural without paraphrase |
| 12:5 | Farewell phrase | "go in-health" (*hygiainōn*) | "go in peace" | "Go well, friend" | **LOGOS** — "go in peace" is idiomatic; EMET's "in health" is literal but PNEUMA adds "friend" not in source |
| 12:6 | How to publish God's deeds | "The-words of God make-known gloriously" | "Proclaim the words of God with honor" | "Shout God's deeds from the rooftops" | **LOGOS** — PNEUMA's idiom is interpretive; EMET's word order is awkward |
| 12:8 | *Eleēmosyna* rendering | Preserved as Greek "eleēmosyna" | "almsgiving" | "Giving to those in need" | **LOGOS** — "almsgiving" is the established translation term; EMET's Greek is scholarly but disrupts reading; PNEUMA loses specificity |
| 12:9 | Who receives life | "Those-who-do eleēmosyna and righteousness will-be-filled with-life" | "Those who give alms and live righteously will be filled with life" | "Those who are merciful, who live justly — they will be filled with life" | **LOGOS** — preserves the two-element structure of the Greek; PNEUMA's paraphrase is valid but loses *eleēmosyna* |
| 12:11 | Angel's disclosure opening | "I-have-said and I-have-hidden" | "I have spoken and I have kept it hidden" | "I can't keep the truth from you any longer" | **LOGOS** — preserves the formal self-referential structure; PNEUMA's dramatic paraphrase loses the echo of v. 7 |
| 12:13 | Tobit's burial act | no qualifying phrase | "without hesitation" | "every act of faithfulness" | **LOGOS** — "without hesitation" draws from the narrative logic; EMET omits, PNEUMA over-expands |
| 12:15 | Core angelophany — Raphael's function | "holy-angels who-present the-prayers of the-holy-ones and enter before the-Glory" | "holy angels who present the prayers of the holy ones and enter before the Glory of the Holy One" | "seven holy angels who stand in the presence of God, who carry the prayers of his people before the Glory" | **LOGOS** — most complete and accurate; PNEUMA's "stand in the presence of God" is harmonization (Luke 1:19), not Sinaiticus; EMET's hyphenation fine but LOGOS reads better |
| 12:18 | Raphael's motivation | "not of my-[own] grace did-I come" | "not of my own accord" | "not...on my own initiative" | **LOGOS** — "accord" captures the Greek *charis/boule* nexus; EMET's "grace" is a possible but odd rendering here |
| 12:19 | Vision clarification | "it-was a-vision you-were-seeing" | "you were seeing a vision" | "What you saw was a vision" | **PNEUMA** — most natural English; the inversion in LOGOS/EMET is grammatically fine but slightly stiff |
| 12:20 | Raphael's ascent | "I-am-ascending to-the-one-who-sent me" | "I am ascending to him who sent me" | "I am returning to the one who sent me" | **LOGOS/EMET** — *anabainō* = "ascend," not merely "return"; the vertical motion is significant angelologically |
| 12:22 | Witnesses' response | "a-messenger of God appeared to-them" | "an angel of God had appeared to them" | "an angel of God had appeared to them in the flesh" | **LOGOS** — PNEUMA's "in the flesh" (*en sarki*) is not in the Sinaiticus text at this point and introduces later theological freight |

---

## Thematic Notes

**The *eleēmosyna* cluster (vv. 8–10):** The most significant translation debate in the chapter. EMET preserves the Greek term throughout to signal its special status; LOGOS normalizes to "almsgiving"; PNEUMA unpacks the meaning dynamically. SOPHIA rules for LOGOS because *eleēmosyna* in Tobit functions as a technical term for the practice of charitable giving as a life-saving virtue — "almsgiving" is the closest stable English equivalent.

**The angelophany formula (v. 15):** This is among the most significant angel-identification formulas in ancient literature, paralleled in Luke 1:19 ("I am Gabriel, who stands before God"). The Sinaiticus text names Raphael as one of *hepta angelōn hagiōn* who *paristanousin* (present/stand before) and *eiserchontai* (enter) *enōpion tēs doxēs tou Hagiou*. The indirect reference ("the Glory of the Holy One" rather than "God") reflects the reverence characteristic of Tobit's theology throughout.

**Disagreement count: 12**

— SOPHIA
